reference.source: Standard gynaecology textbook and hysteroscopy guidance
clinicalPearls: An endometrial polyp is a localised, usually benign overgrowth of endometrial glands and stroma projecting into the uterine cavity, and many are asymptomatic incidental findings
When symptomatic they most often cause abnormal uterine bleeding, including intermenstrual, heavy, or postcoital bleeding, and are a recognised cause of postmenopausal bleeding
They are also associated with subfertility and may be found during investigation of failure to conceive
Transvaginal ultrasound, ideally in the early proliferative phase, may show a focal endometrial thickening or a feeding vessel, and saline infusion sonography or hysteroscopy improves detection
Hysteroscopy allows both diagnosis and treatment, and polypectomy with histological examination is the definitive step
Any endometrial polyp presenting with postmenopausal bleeding must be assessed within a structured postmenopausal-bleeding pathway to exclude endometrial hyperplasia or carcinoma
The risk of malignancy within a polyp is low overall but rises with age, postmenopausal status, larger size, and the presence of bleeding, so histology is important
Asymptomatic small polyps in premenopausal women may occasionally be observed, whereas symptomatic or higher-risk polyps are usually removed
reference.pathophysiology: Endometrial polyps arise from focal, hormonally responsive proliferation of endometrial glands and stroma, typically with a fibrous core and a central feeding vessel, forming a sessile or pedunculated mass that projects into the uterine cavity. Local overexpression of oestrogen receptors relative to progesterone receptors and reduced apoptosis are thought to favour their growth, which is why they are more common in states of unopposed or excess oestrogen and in women taking selective oestrogen receptor modulators. Bleeding results from the fragile surface epithelium and its vasculature. Although the overwhelming majority are benign, foci of hyperplasia or, less commonly, carcinoma can occur within a polyp, particularly after the menopause.
additionalDifferentials: Intrauterine adhesions or other focal endometrial lesions
Cervical polyp prolapsing into the cavity
additionalInvestigations: Transvaginal ultrasound to assess endometrial thickness and focal lesions
Saline infusion sonography (sonohysterography) to delineate intracavitary lesions
Diagnostic hysteroscopy with directed removal and histology
Endometrial sampling to assess the surrounding endometrium, especially with postmenopausal bleeding
Assessment of risk factors such as tamoxifen use, obesity, and unopposed oestrogen exposure
redFlags: Postmenopausal bleeding, mandating exclusion of endometrial hyperplasia or carcinoma
Rapidly growing or large polyp, particularly in an older woman
Atypical hyperplasia or malignancy on histology
Persistent bleeding despite apparently benign imaging
reference.prognosis: The prognosis is excellent for the great majority, which are benign and cured by removal; symptoms such as abnormal bleeding usually resolve after polypectomy, though polyps can recur, and the small minority harbouring hyperplasia or carcinoma require appropriate onward management.
pitfalls: Failing to obtain histology and missing malignancy within an apparently benign polyp
Not investigating postmenopausal bleeding fully because a polyp seems to explain it
Relying on ultrasound alone when saline sonography or hysteroscopy would clarify the diagnosis
Overlooking tamoxifen or unopposed oestrogen as contributing factors
Assuming all polyps need removal without weighing symptoms and risk in young, asymptomatic women
references: Standard gynaecology reference text on abnormal uterine bleeding
Hysteroscopy and postmenopausal bleeding management guidance
management: Hysteroscopic polypectomy with histological examination is the definitive treatment, particularly for symptomatic polyps
Expectant management is reasonable for small asymptomatic polyps in premenopausal women, as some regress spontaneously
Send all removed polyps for histology to exclude endometrial hyperplasia or carcinoma, especially after the menopause
Investigate any polyp presenting with postmenopausal bleeding through a structured postmenopausal-bleeding pathway
Address associated risk factors, reviewing tamoxifen use and unopposed oestrogen exposure and managing obesity
Counsel on the possibility of recurrence and arrange gynaecology follow-up if abnormal bleeding persists
